lessons.title: Structured discovery and requirement gathering
lessons.eli5: Before a builder draws a house, they ask who will live there, what the budget is, and what the local rules allow. Discovery is the same for an AI system: you find out the real problem, the limits and what "good" looks like before choosing any technology.
lessons.body:
## Why discovery comes first

Most failed AI projects do not fail because the model was weak. They fail because the team built the wrong thing, for the wrong user, against a goal nobody wrote down. Task 6.1 tests whether you can turn a vague request ("we want an AI agent for support") into requirements you can design against and test.

The exam rewards an architect who **asks before building**. When a question describes a team that jumped straight to a model or a framework, the defensible answer usually goes back to the missing requirement.

## The discovery checklist

General industry practice, adapted to LLM systems. Capture each item before you pick a pattern or a model.

| Area | Questions to ask | Why it matters for a Claude design |
|---|---|---|
| Business goal | What decision or outcome changes? How is it measured today? | Decides whether AI is even the right tool |
| Users and workflow | Who uses the output, and what do they do next? | Decides the interface: chat, batch report, inline tool |
| Inputs and data | Where does the data live? How fresh, how messy, who owns it? | Drives RAG vs tools vs long context, and the governance scope |
| Latency | Does someone wait for the answer? Seconds, minutes, overnight? | Synchronous API vs Message Batches; model size |
| Volume and cost | Requests per day, peak load, budget per task | Model tier, caching, batching |
| Compliance and risk | Regulated data? Who can see outputs? | Data flow, retention, human review gates |
| Failure tolerance | What does a wrong answer cost? Who catches it? | Human-in-the-loop, confidence routing, escalation |
| Success metrics | How will we know it works, as a number? | Becomes the eval suite |

## Make success criteria testable

Anthropic's evaluation docs say good success criteria are **specific, measurable, achievable and relevant**, and they should usually cover **several dimensions**, not one. "The bot should be accurate" is not a requirement. Compare:

| Vague | Testable |
|---|---|
| "Accurate answers" | "At least N% of answers on a 300-question labelled set match the reference" |
| "Fast" | "95th percentile response under X seconds for interactive chat" |
| "Safe" | "Zero responses that disclose another customer's data on the red-team set" |
| "Cheaper than today" | "Cost per resolved ticket below the current human-handled cost" |

The numbers come from the stakeholders and from baseline measurement, not from the architect's guess. Agreeing on them **before** design is the key move: it gives you an eval target, a way to settle arguments later, and a definition of done.

## Techniques that work

- **Shadow the workflow.** Watch the people who do the task now. The hidden steps (checking a second system, phoning a colleague) become tools or escalation paths.
- **Collect real examples early.** Ask for 50 to 200 real inputs with the expected outputs. They seed the eval set and expose edge cases no interview will surface.
- **Separate must-haves from nice-to-haves.** Use a simple priority label per requirement so trade-off talks later have a shared reference.
- **Name the non-goals.** "Version 1 will not issue refunds" is a requirement. It also shrinks the tool surface, which helps least privilege.
- **Identify every stakeholder.** End users, their managers, security, legal, data owners, operations. A missing stakeholder is a late blocker.

## Worked example

A logistics firm asks for "an agent that answers carrier emails". Discovery finds:

- 70% of emails ask for shipment status, which already exists in an internal API.
- Replies must go out within 4 business hours (current contract terms).
- Emails sometimes contain bank details, so the data-protection lead must approve data flows.
- A wrong delivery date is an annoyance; a wrong customs instruction is a fine.

The design that follows from this is modest. It is a **workflow**, not an open-ended agent: classify the email, call the status API as a tool, draft a reply, and send customs topics to a human. The 4-hour window means you do not need sub-second latency, so a cheaper model and queued processing are both fine. Without discovery, the team might have built a fully autonomous multi-agent system that had a risky tool surface and no measurable goal.

## Start simple, then earn complexity

Anthropic's guidance on building agents recommends finding the simplest solution first and adding complexity only when it clearly improves results. Discovery is where you collect the evidence for that call. If the requirements can be met by one well-prompted call with retrieval, an agent framework is a cost, not a feature.

## Output of discovery

A short, shared **requirements brief**: goal, users, constraints, data sources, risks, non-goals, and the success metrics and how they will be measured. Stakeholders sign it off. It becomes the reference for every later trade-off conversation (task 6.2) and the baseline for the eval suite (task 6.5).
keyTakeaways: Capture goal, users, data sources, latency, volume/cost, compliance, failure tolerance and success metrics before choosing a pattern or model.
Success criteria must be specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, and usually multidimensional (quality, latency, cost, safety).
Agree how success will be evaluated up front; the agreed metrics become the eval suite and settle later disputes.
Real example inputs with expected outputs, collected early, are the best discovery artifact.
Non-goals are requirements: they shrink scope and the tool surface.
Start with the simplest design that meets the requirements; discovery supplies the evidence for adding complexity.
examTips: If a stem shows a team picking a model, framework or multi-agent design before any requirement or metric is defined, the best answer usually restores the missing discovery step.
Look for buried constraints (a reply window, regulated data, who acts on the output). They decide sync vs batch, review gates and pattern choice.
"First step" questions favour clarifying the goal and success metric over building a prototype or running a bake-off.
Prefer answers that turn a vague goal into a measurable one with a baseline.
commonTraps: Accepting "high accuracy" or "fast" as a requirement without a number and a test set.
Choosing the most capable or most autonomous architecture because the customer asked for "an agent".
Interviewing only the sponsor and missing security, legal or data owners until late.
Treating a prototype demo as a substitute for agreed success criteria.

lessons.title: Communicating architectural decisions and trade-offs
lessons.eli5: When you recommend a car to a friend, you do not list engine specs. You say "this one costs a bit more but is much safer and cheaper to run". Explaining architecture works the same way: show the real options and say what each costs and risks in terms the listener cares about.
lessons.body:
## What task 6.2 is really testing

An architect's recommendation is only as good as the decision it enables. Executives, product owners, security reviewers and engineers each care about different things, and each must be able to say yes or no with full information. The exam tests whether you can:

1. present **credible alternatives**, not a single option dressed up as a choice,
2. translate technical properties into **business terms** (cost, risk, time to value, service levels), and
3. record the decision so it can be revisited when circumstances change.

## Translate technical facts into business terms

| Technical statement | Business framing |
|---|---|
| "Opus is more capable than Haiku on multi-step reasoning" | "The larger model cuts escalations on complex cases; it costs more per request, so we use it only for that segment" |
| "Prompt caching gives cache reads at a fraction of input price" | "Reusing our fixed policy text lowers cost and response time for every request" |
| "Message Batches is 50% cheaper but asynchronous, up to 24 hours" | "Overnight reports cost half as much; anything a person is waiting on stays on the real-time path" |
| "Multi-agent research uses far more tokens than a single agent" | "The deeper research mode costs several times more per query, so we offer it only where the answer is worth that" |
| "RAG adds a retrieval step" | "Answers are grounded in our current documents and can cite them; it adds a little latency" |

Every option has a cost, a risk and a benefit. If you can't name all three, you aren't ready to present it.

## A simple options table

Present two to four options against the criteria agreed in discovery. A worked example for an internal policy assistant:

| Criterion | A: Long context, whole handbook in prompt | B: RAG over handbook | C: Tool-using agent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Time to first version | Fastest | Medium | Slowest |
| Cost per query | Highest (large prompt; caching helps) | Low | Variable, often highest |
| Freshness when policies change | Re-deploy prompt | Re-index | Re-index plus tool upkeep |
| Citations / auditability | Possible | Natural | Possible |
| Main risk | Grows past budget as handbook grows | Retrieval misses cause wrong answers | Hard to predict and test |
| **Recommendation** | Pilot only | **Production** | Not justified by requirements |

The recommendation is explicit and tied to the criteria. The rejected options are recorded together with the reasons they were rejected.

## Decision records

A lightweight **architecture decision record (ADR)** is common industry practice and works well for AI systems because models, prices and features change quickly.

```markdown
# ADR-007: Use Message Batches for nightly claim summaries
Status: Accepted (2026-09-14)
Context: 40k claims/night; summaries needed by 08:00; no user waits.
Options: (1) synchronous calls, (2) Message Batches API.
Decision: (2). About 50% lower token cost; completion within 24h fits
  a submit-at-18:00, need-by-08:00 window only with a fallback.
Consequences: Add a fallback that re-runs unfinished items synchronously
  after 06:00. Revisit if the need-by time moves earlier.
Sign-off: Product, Finance, Security (data flow unchanged).
```

Notice the parts: context, options considered, decision, consequences (including new work it creates), and who signed off. A future reader can tell **why** the system is shaped this way and what would trigger a revisit.

## Getting the right sign-offs

The official Professional prep course describes the goal as solutions that "pass security review" and "earn stakeholder sign-off". In practice (general practice):

- **Security** signs off on tool scope, credentials and data paths (least privilege).
- **Legal / compliance** signs off on where data flows, retention and regulated content. Governance follows the actual data flow, not what a contract says.
- **Product / business owner** signs off on the trade-off itself: the quality, cost and latency they are accepting.
- **Operations** signs off on what they will have to monitor and support.

Bring them in when the decision is made, not after the build. A late security review that removes a tool can invalidate a design.

## Communicating uncertainty honestly

LLM behaviour is probabilistic. Say so, with numbers from evals: "On our 400-case test set, option B answered 91% correctly and declined 6%; the remaining 3% were wrong, mostly on scanned PDFs." That is more persuasive and more defensible than "it's very accurate". Avoid promising that a prompt change *guarantees* a behaviour. If something must always happen, explain that it will be enforced in code or by a workflow gate.

## How to handle pushback

- **"Just use the biggest model."** Show the eval result per model tier and the cost per task. Often a smaller model plus better retrieval or prompts meets the bar.
- **"Make it fully autonomous."** Show the failure cost from discovery and propose staged autonomy: human review first, then remove review for categories where evals show it is safe.
- **"Can we skip the review step to hit the deadline?"** Restate the risk in business terms and record the decision, including who accepted the risk.
keyTakeaways: Present two to four credible options against the criteria agreed in discovery, with a clear recommendation.
Frame every option in business terms: cost, risk, time to value, service level, auditability.
Record decisions in a short decision record: context, options, decision, consequences, sign-off, revisit trigger.
Bring security, legal/compliance, product and operations into the decision, not after the build.
Quote eval numbers to communicate non-determinism honestly; never promise a prompt guarantees behaviour.
examTips: The best answer usually compares alternatives against agreed criteria; a single option presented as a fait accompli is a distractor.
Prefer answers that express trade-offs in business consequences (cost per task, SLA, risk) over raw technical specs for a non-technical audience.
When a stakeholder demands a guarantee, the right response moves the guarantee into code or workflow and explains that, rather than promising a stronger prompt.
If a decision touches data flows or tool permissions, expect security and legal sign-off to be part of the correct answer.
commonTraps: Leading with model specs, benchmarks or jargon to an executive audience.
Hiding the downsides of the recommended option to win approval.
Treating "bigger model" as the default answer to any quality complaint.
Documenting only the chosen option, so nobody knows why the alternatives were rejected.
Getting compliance sign-off based on the vendor contract instead of the actual data flow.

lessons.title: Feedback loops, expectation alignment and SLAs
lessons.eli5: A pizza shop that promises "30 minutes or free" must know its ovens and drivers can actually do that. An AI system is the same: only promise speeds and accuracy your design can really deliver, then keep checking with customers whether it still meets their needs.
lessons.body:
## Two jobs in one task statement

Task 6.3 combines two related skills:

1. **Expectation alignment.** Stakeholders need an accurate picture of what the system will and will not do, including the fact that LLM output varies.
2. **Feedback loops.** Real usage keeps revealing new needs and failures. You need a regular way to capture them and feed them into the system.

SLAs (service level agreements) sit in between. They are the written promise, so they must match what the architecture can deliver.

## Setting expectations about non-determinism

- **Use eval results, not adjectives.** "On 500 representative tickets, 88% were resolved correctly, 9% escalated, 3% wrong" sets a realistic expectation and a baseline for improvement.
- **Explain error types, not just rates.** A 3% error rate that is all harmless formatting slips differs from 3% wrong refund amounts. Anthropic's eval docs model this in an example criterion that separates errors that merely cause inconvenience from egregious ones, so report severity as well as rate.
- **Say what is guaranteed and how.** A schema-valid output format can be guaranteed with structured outputs (`output_config.format`) or strict tool schemas; whether the field values are *correct* cannot. Business rules that must always hold go in code or workflow gates. Tone and judgement are probabilistic and are measured, not promised.
- **Make the human role explicit.** If people review outputs, say what they review, how fast, and what happens when they disagree.

## Writing SLAs the architecture can meet

Define service level objectives first (internal targets), then commit to an SLA with headroom. Each one must trace to a design property.

| SLA dimension | Example commitment | Architecture that supports it |
|---|---|---|
| Latency (interactive) | p95 under a few seconds | Synchronous Messages API, streaming, right-sized model, prompt caching for fixed prefixes |
| Turnaround (bulk) | Results by next business morning | Message Batches API (up to 24 h) plus a synchronous fallback for stragglers |
| Quality | At least X% correct on the agreed eval set, re-measured monthly | Eval suite and regression runs on every change |
| Availability | Degraded mode during provider errors | Retries with backoff, queueing, graceful fallback message |
| Escalation | Human response within N hours for escalated cases | Staffed review queue, routing rules |

### The classic mismatch: batch vs real time

The Message Batches API gives a **50% discount** on input and output tokens. It processes requests asynchronously; most batches finish in under an hour, but there is **no latency guarantee** for individual requests. Processing is capped at **24 hours**: results are released when every request has finished or when 24 hours have passed, whichever comes first, and any request still unprocessed at that point **expires** (you are not billed for it, but you must resubmit it). Results stay downloadable for 29 days. So:

- Never promise real-time or same-minute results on a batch pipeline.
- Do use batches for overnight reports, backfills, bulk classification and evaluation runs.
- A blocking step (a pre-merge check, a live chat reply) stays synchronous.

### SLA arithmetic

Suppose the commitment is "every uploaded contract summarised within 36 hours", using batches. Worst case = time waiting for the next batch submission + up to 24 h processing + your own pre- and post-processing. To stay inside 36 h you need submission windows well under 12 hours apart. Leave a buffer for retries of failed items, for example every 6 to 8 hours. If the business later tightens the SLA to 4 hours, batching no longer fits and the cost model changes. That is a renegotiation, not a tweak.

## Building the feedback loop

```text
users / reviewers --> feedback capture (thumbs, edits, escalations, tickets)
        |                              |
        v                              v
  production logs  ----->  triage: new failure category?  ---> add cases to eval set
                                       |
                                       v
                       fix (prompt, retrieval, tool, workflow) ---> re-run evals ---> release
                                       |
                                       v
                   stakeholder review: metrics vs SLA, top issues, decisions needed
```

Practical rules (general practice):

- **Capture signals where work already happens.** Reviewer edits and escalations are richer than star ratings.
- **Turn every confirmed failure into an eval case** so it can't silently regress.
- **Hold a regular stakeholder review** with the same small dashboard each time: quality versus target, latency versus SLA, cost per task, top failure categories, open decisions.
- **Close the loop with the people who reported issues.** Tell them what changed. Trust grows when people see their feedback acted on.

## Worked example

A bank's operations team says the document-extraction pilot is "unreliable". Instead of swapping models, the architect pulls the feedback log. 80% of complaints concern one scanned form type with handwritten fields. The architect then:

1. adds 40 of those forms to the eval set,
2. sets a separate, lower accuracy target for handwritten forms and routes them to human review,
3. updates the SLA document so the 99% straight-through target covers typed forms only, and
4. reports the change at the fortnightly review.

The expectation is now accurate, the SLA is achievable, and the remaining gap is visible and owned.

## When expectations and reality diverge

Do not quietly miss the SLA, and do not over-promise to recover. Show the data. Offer options (more human review, a stronger model for one segment, a relaxed target) with their costs, and let the business owner choose. Then record the decision.
keyTakeaways: Set expectations with eval numbers and error types, not adjectives; be explicit about what is guaranteed (schema, code gates) and what is probabilistic.
Every SLA must trace to an architectural property; define internal objectives first and commit with headroom.

Message Batches: 50% cheaper, asynchronous, most batches finish in under an hour but processing is capped at 24 hours (unfinished requests expire and must be resubmitted), no per-request latency guarantee; never promise real time on it.
Do SLA arithmetic: worst case = submission wait + up to 24 h processing + your own processing and retries.
A feedback loop captures real signals, turns confirmed failures into eval cases, and reports against the same dashboard at a regular review.
examTips: If a stem promises interactive or blocking latency on a batch pipeline, the correct answer moves that path to the synchronous API (or changes the promise).
Choose answers that renegotiate or re-scope an SLA with data over answers that silently tune and hope.
Answers that add confirmed production failures to the eval set before fixing them reflect the expected mindset.
Self-reported model confidence or a "be accurate" instruction is not a basis for an SLA; measured eval results are.
commonTraps: Promising "the model will always" do something based on a prompt instruction.
Assuming most-batches-finish-within-an-hour means you can promise one-hour turnaround.
Collecting thumbs-up/down ratings without a process that turns them into fixes and tests.
Fixing the one complaint loudly raised in a meeting without checking whether it represents the main failure category.
Measuring only accuracy and ignoring latency, cost and error severity in SLA reporting.

lessons.title: Documenting architectures and implementation guidance
lessons.eli5: A recipe card on the fridge only helps if the cook actually reads it. Good AI architecture docs explain how the system works for people, and they also put the team's rules where the AI coding tools will load them automatically.
lessons.body:
## Two audiences for documentation

An AI solution's documentation has to serve:

1. **People.** Sponsors, reviewers, the team that operates the system and the team that inherits it.
2. **The AI tools that help build and run it.** Claude Code reads project instruction files, rules and skills. Guidance that lives in those files is **applied**, not just written down.

Task 6.4 tests whether you produce documents that let someone else build, run and change the system safely.

## The core document set

General industry practice, adapted to Claude-based systems:

| Document | Audience | Must contain |
|---|---|---|
| Architecture overview | Everyone | Purpose, context diagram, data flow from input to output, pattern chosen (workflow, agent, augmented LLM) and why |
| Decision records (ADRs) | Architects, reviewers | Options, decision, consequences, sign-offs, revisit triggers |
| Prompt and model register | Engineers, operators | Model IDs in use, prompt versions, tools and their scopes, eval scores per version |
| Data-flow and governance sheet | Security, legal | What data goes where, retention, who can see outputs, human review points |
| Runbook | On-call / operations | Dashboards, alerts, known failure modes, step-by-step responses, escalation contacts |
| Implementation guide | Builders | Conventions, repo layout, how to add a tool, how to run evals, definition of done |
| Handoff guide | Receiving team | Open risks, outstanding work, owners, how to get help |

### LLM-specific content people forget

- **Exact model identifiers** and the date they were last evaluated. Models get deprecated and retired, so this is how you know what to re-test.
- **Prompt versions** stored in source control with the eval results that justified them.
- **Tool inventory** with each tool's permissions. This is the least-privilege record that security reviews.
- **Known limitations**: input types that score poorly, languages not tested, the cases that always go to a human.
- **Eval suite location and pass thresholds**, so anyone can check a change before release.

## A runbook entry that actually helps

```markdown
### Symptom: answers cite last quarter's policy
Likely cause: retrieval index not refreshed after the policy upload.
Check: index build timestamp on the RAG dashboard vs the document store.
Fix: re-run the index job; then run the "policy-freshness" eval subset.
Do NOT: switch models or edit the system prompt first; the model is
  answering faithfully from stale retrieved text.
Escalate: data platform on-call if the index job fails twice.
```

Good runbook entries go from symptom to cause, check, fix and escalation. They also warn against the tempting wrong fix. That matches how the Professional exam frames diagnosis: find the root cause, such as retrieval, before blaming the model.

## Encoding guidance where Claude Code applies it

For teams that build with Claude Code, the implementation guide should not just be a wiki page. Put conventions where the tool loads them:

| Mechanism | Location | When it loads | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Project CLAUDE.md | `./CLAUDE.md` or `./.claude/CLAUDE.md` (committed) | At session start | Build/test commands, architecture summary, team-wide conventions |
| Path-scoped rules | `.claude/rules/*.md` with `paths:` globs | When Claude reads a matching file | Conventions for specific areas, e.g. all `**/*.test.ts` files |
| Skills | `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | On demand, by name or when relevant | Repeatable procedures: "add a new tool", "run the eval suite" |
| Personal notes | `CLAUDE.local.md` (git-ignored) | At session start, for you only | Individual preferences that should not bind the team |

```markdown
<!-- .claude/rules/prompts.md -->
---
paths:
  - "prompts/**/*.md"
---
- Every prompt change needs a matching entry in prompts/CHANGELOG.md.
- Run `npm run eval -- --suite=regression` before opening a PR.
- Never put customer data in example blocks; use the fixtures in evals/fixtures/.
```

Remember the boundary. Instruction files guide behaviour, but they don't **enforce** it. Anything that must always happen (block a secret from being committed, require evals to pass) belongs in a hook, CI check or permission rule. Document the guidance and also enforce the critical parts.

## Keep documentation alive

- **Docs live next to the code** and change in the same pull request as the code they describe.
- **Every ADR has a revisit trigger** (a price change, a new model, a volume threshold).
- **Generate what you can.** Tool inventories and model registers can be produced from config, so they don't drift.
- **Test the handoff.** Ask someone outside the build team to follow the runbook for one incident scenario. Each place they get stuck is a documentation bug.

## Worked example

A consultancy hands an internal claims assistant to a client's platform team. The handoff pack contains the architecture overview, six ADRs, the data-flow sheet signed by the client's DPO, a runbook with eight symptom entries, and the repo's CLAUDE.md, rules and two skills (`/add-claim-type` and `/run-evals`). Three weeks later the client adds a new claim type on its own. The skill walks the engineer through schema, prompt, tests and eval cases in order. No consultant call is needed, and that independence is the goal of task 6.4.
keyTakeaways: Document for people (overview, ADRs, data-flow sheet, runbook, handoff guide) and for the tools (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills).
LLM-specific docs must record exact model IDs, prompt versions with eval scores, the tool inventory with scopes, known limitations and the eval suite with thresholds.
Runbooks go symptom, likely cause, check, fix, escalation, and warn against the tempting wrong fix.
Put team conventions in committed CLAUDE.md, path-scoped .claude/rules and shared skills so they are applied automatically; personal preferences go in CLAUDE.local.md.
Instruction files guide but do not enforce; must-always rules belong in hooks, CI or permissions.
examTips: When new team members "don't follow the conventions", look for an answer that moves guidance from a personal or external location into committed project config.
Conventions for files scattered across folders point to .claude/rules with paths globs, not a subdirectory CLAUDE.md.
A runbook-style answer that checks retrieval or data freshness before changing the model matches the root-cause mindset.
Prefer documentation that lives with the code and is updated in the same change over a separate wiki.
commonTraps: Assuming a well-written wiki page means the AI coding tool follows the conventions.
Putting team-wide instructions in a user-level file (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) that teammates never load.
Treating CLAUDE.md text as an enforcement mechanism for security rules.
Recording "we use the latest model" instead of an exact model identifier and its last evaluation date.
Handoff packs that describe the design but have no runbook or owner list.

lessons.title: Supporting the lifecycle: discovery to iteration
lessons.eli5: A garden is never "finished": you plan it, plant it, hand it to someone to water, watch what grows, and adjust. An AI system has the same cycle, and the measuring stick (the eval tests) tells you what to change next.
lessons.body:
## The five phases

Task 6.5 names them: **discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration**. For LLM systems the cycle never really ends, because the inputs, the business and the models all change.

| Phase | Key activities | Exit criteria (what "done" means) |
|---|---|---|
| Discovery | Goals, users, constraints, data, success metrics, example set | Signed requirements brief; agreed metrics; seed eval set |
| Design | Pattern and model choice, prompts, tools, retrieval, guardrails, review gates | ADRs signed off; eval suite runs; pilot meets thresholds |
| Handoff | Docs, runbooks, CLAUDE.md/rules/skills, training, ownership transfer | Receiving team runs evals and handles a drill incident alone |
| Monitoring | Quality sampling, latency, cost, errors, escalations, drift | Dashboards and alerts live; owners named; SLA reported |
| Iteration | Triage failures, add eval cases, change, re-run evals, release | Change beats or matches baseline on the full suite; stakeholders informed |

## Evals are the spine

The eval suite links every phase:

- **Discovery** produces the first labelled examples and the success thresholds.
- **Design** uses evals to choose between options (model tier, retrieval vs long context).
- **Handoff** passes the suite to the new owners as the definition of "working".
- **Monitoring** samples production traffic and grades it the same way, so production numbers can be compared with test numbers.
- **Iteration** adds every confirmed failure as a new case and gates releases on the full suite.

A change that hasn't been run against the suite is a guess. This is the habit the exam keeps rewarding: measure, change one thing, measure again.

## Monitoring for LLM systems

Classic metrics still matter (error rates, latency, cost). LLM systems also need:

- **Output-quality sampling.** Grade a slice of production outputs with code checks, an LLM grader with a rubric, or human review, matched to the risk.
- **Escalation and override rates.** A rising human-override rate is often the first sign of drift.
- **Input drift.** New document types, languages or topics that the eval set doesn't cover.
- **Token usage per task.** Silent growth (longer histories, bigger retrieved chunks) erodes the cost case.
- **Stop reasons and tool errors.** For example, a spike in truncated outputs (`max_tokens`) or failing tool calls.

## Planning for model and version changes

Models move through lifecycle states. Anthropic's model-deprecation page lists **Active, Legacy, Deprecated and Retired**. Requests to a retired model fail. Anthropic gives **at least 60 days' notice** before retiring a publicly released model and recommends testing replacements well before the retirement date. Partner platforms such as Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud set their own schedules.

What this means for the lifecycle:

1. **Pin exact model IDs** in config and record them in the model register.
2. **Watch deprecation notices** and put the retirement date on the roadmap the day it is announced.
3. **Treat a model upgrade as a release.** Run the full eval suite on the candidate, compare quality, latency and cost, and check prompt behaviour. Newer models can change defaults or reject parameters older ones accepted.
4. **Roll out gradually.** Shadow-run or A/B the new model on a slice of traffic, then cut over.
5. **Tell stakeholders.** A model change can shift tone, length or cost. Treat it like any other change review.

The same discipline applies to prompt changes, new tools, retrieval re-indexing and policy updates. Each is a change that re-runs evals and goes through a short review.

## Handoff done well

Handoff is where many projects lose quality. Good practice (general):

- Transfer **ownership**, not just files: named owners for prompts, evals, data pipelines and on-call.
- Hand over **working tooling**: the eval runner, dashboards, the CLAUDE.md, rules and skills that make the team's conventions automatic.
- Run a **drill**: the receiving team diagnoses a staged incident with the runbook while the builders watch.
- Agree a **support window** and a final review against the original success metrics.

## Worked example: one loop around the cycle

A support-triage workflow has run for four months. Monitoring shows the override rate climbing from 6% to 14% in two weeks. Triage finds a new product line launched with terms the classifier has never seen.

1. **Discovery (mini):** confirm with the support lead which categories the new product needs.
2. **Design:** add the categories and few-shot examples to the prompt; add 60 labelled tickets to the eval set.
3. **Eval:** the new prompt holds on the old cases and reaches the target on the new ones.
4. **Release:** ship to 20% of traffic first, then to all.
5. **Monitoring:** the override rate returns to baseline. The change and its numbers go into the stakeholder review and the prompt register.

There was no model swap and no rebuild. The system improved through one cycle of measure, change and verify.

## Recertification-style change reviews

For regulated or high-risk systems, schedule a periodic review even when nothing seems broken. Re-run the full eval suite, re-confirm data flows with compliance, re-check tool permissions, and confirm the model is not deprecated. This catches slow drift that day-to-day monitoring normalises.
keyTakeaways: Lifecycle phases: discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration, each with explicit exit criteria.
The eval suite connects every phase; no change ships without running it.
Monitor LLM-specific signals: sampled output quality, override/escalation rate, input drift, tokens per task, stop reasons and tool errors.
Models go Active, Legacy, Deprecated, Retired; Anthropic gives at least 60 days notice before retiring public models, and requests to retired models fail.
Treat model upgrades, prompt changes and re-indexing as releases: re-run evals, roll out gradually, inform stakeholders.
Handoff transfers ownership and working tooling, proven by a drill, not just documents.
examTips: For "a model is being deprecated" stems, the best answer runs the existing eval suite on the replacement before cutting over, not a blind ID swap or an indefinite delay.
When production quality degrades, prefer answers that diagnose from monitoring data and add cases to the eval set over immediate model changes.
A rising human-override or escalation rate is a monitoring signal of drift; expect it to be the trigger in iteration questions.
Correct answers usually close the loop: measure, change, re-measure, communicate.
commonTraps: Treating launch as the end of the project, with no monitoring owner or eval gate.
Using a floating "latest" model alias in production and being surprised by behaviour changes.
Assuming a newer model is a drop-in replacement without testing.
Monitoring only uptime and latency, never output quality.
Handoffs that transfer documents but no ownership, tooling or drill.
